208.title: Adapting Guidelines for Country use
208.content: . The following page provides a reference to resources that can guide countries in adapting the guidelines for country use. To implement WHO recommendations in country settings, governments must interpret and then adapt the content in line with local policies, procedures, and digital tools. This implementation guide provides the generic content required in digital systems, independently of a specific software application and with the intention that countries can adapt it to meet local needs. WHO guidelines articulate and endorse rigorously tested recommendations for health interventions to be adopted within country programs. When applied correctly and consistently, guideline recommendations save lives. To ensure that countries can effectively benefit from digital health investments, the SMART Guidelines approach is intended to facilitate the accurate reflection of WHO’s clinical, public health and data use guidelines in the digital systems that countries are adopting. For more on layers of knowledge representation and how they are used in WHO’s SMART Guidelines approach, see WHO’s SMART Guidelines and this Lancet article. The standards-based technical artifacts in this implementation guide are at the third layer of knowledge representation (L3: Machine-readable recommendations). It provides code necessary for software developers to incorporate standardised logic from WHO guidelines into digital systems, testable for conformance to standards including fidelity to recommendations. A standards-based technical implementation guide builds on operational (L2) by mapping L2 content to value sets and Health Level Seven International Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR) standards. Alongside data standards from L2, this allows for semantic and syntactic interoperability at scale. The logic derived from guidelines, which might include clinical decision support and calculations for performance indicators, which may be encoded into Clinical Quality Language (CQL). This ensures that key indicators can be consistently extracted to support patient care, as well as case surveillance and programme monitoring. The machine-readable representations in this implementation guide are intended for adaptation into countries’ digital health service delivery and reporting systems. Digital solutions comprising L3 machine-readable recommendations may then be testable for conformance to interoperability standards. The fourth layer (L4: Executable—reference applications and services) focuses on software applications and services within a digital ecosystem. It is intended to include executable reference software that accurately represents the intentions, operational, and functional requirements of the WHO recommendations; addresses user and health system needs; and comprises machine-readable data and calculations within interoperability standards, as documented in the L1–L3 layers. As a fully functional application, it is intended to serve as a generic starting point, ready to be localised to the specific operational context of the users, population, and health system within which it is deployed. Additional products at this layer include terminology services to support consistent data representation for interoperability; reusable software libraries including software development kits; application programming interfaces; and function as a service to support updates to FHIR content and capabilities across subscribed digital systems. 1018.title: Business Processes
1018.content: . This page describes the core business processes and workflows for the Personal Health Wallet (PHW) Implementation Guide, integrating IHE IT Infrastructure Privacy Consent on FHIR (PCF) v1.1.0 (https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/1.1.0/) and IHE IT Infrastructure Verifiable Health Links (VHL) v1.0.0-comment (https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/VHL/1.0.0-comment/). A business process is a set of related activities or tasks performed together by system actors and human personas to achieve a health information exchange objective. Each workflow below is authored in BPMN 2.0 (input/business-processes/PHW.A.bpmn, input/business-processes/PHW.B.bpmn, input/business-processes/PHW.C.bpmn) with full BPMN Diagram Interchange (bpmndi:BPMNDiagram) layout and rendered to SVG (input/images/PHW.A.svg, input/images/PHW.B.svg, input/images/PHW.C.svg). The data sharing agreement processes D to H, below, take the same form. Architectural Principles . | Trust-Anchor Neutrality: Every process models PKI key publication ([ITI-YY1]) and trust list retrieval ([ITI-YY2]) against an abstract Trust Anchor actor (https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/VHL/ActorDefinition/TrustAnchor). The WHO Global Digital Health Certification Network (GDHCN) is one possible Trust Anchor implementation among others (such as national health PKI roots, regional cross-border trust networks, or bilateral federation anchors). | Explicit IHE PCF and VHL Transaction Binding: Every cross-actor task names its normative IHE transaction ([ITI-108] Access Consent, [ITI-YY1] Submit PKI Material with DID, [ITI-YY2] Retrieve Trust List with DID, [ITI-YY3] Generate VHL, [ITI-YY4] Provide VHL, [ITI-YY5] Retrieve Manifest). | No IHE IUA Claim: Consent management and enforcement operate over IHE PCF [ITI-108] Access Consent and VHL [ITI-YY1]–[ITI-YY5] without claiming conformance to IHE Internet User Authorization (IUA [ITI-71]). | | Three-Valued Consent Decision and PROV-O Provenance: During VHL redemption (Process C), patient privacy consent directives retrieved via [ITI-108] are translated to W3C ODRL 2.2 policies (consentToOdrl()) and evaluated via three-valued decide() (permit | deny | unknown), recording a W3C PROV-O prov:Activity citing Consent.id and Consent.meta.versionId. | . | . Overview of Key Business Processes . The following table summarizes the three BPMN 2.0 consent and Verifiable Health Link business processes defined in this Implementation Guide. The data sharing agreement processes are summarized in their own section below. | # | Process Name | Process ID | Personas | Objectives | . | A | Record and Manage Patient Privacy Consent | PHW.A | Holder, Consent Recorder, Consent Registry | Capture, update, or revoke a patient privacy consent directive (IHE.PCF.consentBasic or IHE.PCF.consentIntermediate) in a PCF Consent Registry via [ITI-108] Access Consent (Post, Put, Delete). | . | B | Issue Consent-Backed Verifiable Health Link | PHW.B | Holder, VHL Sharer, Consent Registry, Trust Anchor | Register VHL Sharer signing keys with a Trust Anchor ([ITI-YY1]), verify or record active patient consent ([ITI-108]), and generate a signed Verifiable Health Link ([ITI-YY3]) stored in the Holder’s Personal Health Wallet. | . | C | Present and Redeem Verifiable Health Link with PCF Consent Enforcement | PHW.C | Holder, VHL Receiver, Trust Anchor, VHL Sharer, Consent Registry | Present a VHL ([ITI-YY4]), verify cryptographic trust via a Trust Anchor ([ITI-YY2]), request the manifest ([ITI-YY5]), query active PCF Consent ([ITI-108]), and enforce three-valued (permit / deny / unknown) ODRL consent evaluation with PROV-O provenance. | . Workflows . A. Record and Manage Patient Privacy Consent . | Process ID: PHW.A | BPMN Source: input/business-processes/PHW.A.bpmn | Objective: Capture, update, or revoke a patient privacy consent directive (IHE.PCF.consentBasic or IHE.PCF.consentIntermediate) in a PCF Consent Registry using the IHE PCF Access Consent [ITI-108] transaction (Post, Put, Delete), trust-anchor neutral and with no IUA claim. | . | Activity ID | Lane / Actor | Task Name | IHE PCF / VHL Transaction & Conformance Profile | . | PHW.A.1 | VHL Holder (Patient / Personal Health Wallet) | Select base policy & disclosure scope (PCF Basic / Intermediate Consent) | Selection of base policy (Consent.policy.uri), PCFPurposeOfUseVS purpose of use, authorized actors, validity period, and clinical data scope | . | PHW.A.2 | PCF Consent Recorder (Wallet / VHL Sharer) | Construct FHIR Consent & Provenance (IHE.PCF.consentBasic / Intermediate) | https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/PCF/StructureDefinition/IHE.PCF.consentBasic, IHE.PCF.consentIntermediate, IHE.PCF.provenance | . | PHW.A.3 | PCF Consent Recorder (Wallet / VHL Sharer) | Create consent directive [ITI-108] Access Consent: Post | [ITI-108] Access Consent (POST [base]/Consent or transaction Bundle with Provenance) | . | PHW.A.4 | PCF Consent Recorder (Wallet / VHL Sharer) | Update or revoke directive [ITI-108] Access Consent: Put / Delete | [ITI-108] Access Consent (PUT [base]/Consent/[id] or DELETE [base]/Consent/[id]) | . | PHW.A.5 | PCF Consent Registry | Validate, version & persist Consent + Provenance [ITI-108] Access Consent | [ITI-108] Access Consent responder (IHE.PCF.consentRegistry), assigning Consent.id and Consent.meta.versionId | . | PHW.A.6 | VHL Holder (Patient / Personal Health Wallet) | Confirm recorded Consent.id & versionId [ITI-108] Access Consent response | [ITI-108] Access Consent response (201 Created / 200 OK) | . Consent rules, from the person’s side . Process A is the person-side view of the data sharing agreement’s consent process (P9). The owner set four rules on 2026-10-30: . | Legal basis. Only an agreement whose legal basis is consent asks for consent. Treatment, public-health law and research waivers do not rest on consent. | Version pinning. The person consents to one fixed version of the agreement: Consent.policy.uri is that version’s URL. If the agreement is amended to widen use, the new version needs new consent. An amendment that narrows use does not. | Plain language. The person is shown the agreement’s plain-language summary, published and hashed with the agreement. That summary is what they consent to (task PHW.A.1). | Scale. Where the person has recorded nothing, the jurisdiction’s chosen PCF implicit default policy applies: opt-in (for example Policy-deny) or opt-out (for example Policy-basic-normal or Policy-all-normal). Registry lookups may be cached (task PHW.C.5), but withdrawing a Consent (status becomes inactive, task PHW.A.4) ends every cached result that holds it at once. | . B. Issue Consent-Backed Verifiable Health Link . | Process ID: PHW.B | BPMN Source: input/business-processes/PHW.B.bpmn | Objective: Publish VHL Sharer PKI signing keys to an abstract Trust Anchor ([ITI-YY1]), verify or record an active patient privacy consent directive ([ITI-108]), and generate a signed Verifiable Health Link ([ITI-YY3]) for storage in the Holder’s Personal Health Wallet. Trust-anchor neutral (WHO GDHCN is one possible Trust Anchor among others). | . | Activity ID | Lane / Actor | Task Name | IHE PCF / VHL Transaction & Conformance Profile | . | PHW.B.1 | VHL Sharer (grouped with PCF Consent Recorder) | Submit Sharer PKI signing key [ITI-YY1] Submit PKI Material with DID | [ITI-YY1] Submit PKI Material with DID (https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/VHL/Requirements/PublishPKIMaterial) | . | PHW.B.2 | Trust Anchor (e.g. GDHCN, national, or regional anchor) | Publish key in Trust Anchor trust list [ITI-YY1] (GDHCN or other anchor) | [ITI-YY1] Submit PKI Material with DID (https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/VHL/CapabilityStatement/IHE.VHL.TrustAnchor) | . | PHW.B.3 | VHL Holder (Patient / Personal Health Wallet) | Request VHL generation [ITI-YY3] Generate VHL ($generate-vhl) | [ITI-YY3] Generate VHL (https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/VHL/OperationDefinition/GenerateVHL) | . | PHW.B.4 | VHL Sharer (grouped with PCF Consent Recorder) | Query or record active Consent [ITI-108] Access Consent: Search / Post | [ITI-108] Access Consent (GET [base]/Consent?patient=...&status=active or POST [base]/Consent) | . | PHW.B.5 | PCF Consent Registry | Return active PCF Consent (Consent.id + versionId) [ITI-108] Access Consent | [ITI-108] Access Consent responder (IHE.PCF.consentRegistry) | . | PHW.B.6 | VHL Sharer (grouped with PCF Consent Recorder) | Assemble & sign VHL payload bound to Consent [ITI-YY3] Generate VHL | [ITI-YY3] Generate VHL (IHE.VHL.VHLSharer), signing with [ITI-YY1] key material | . | PHW.B.7 | VHL Holder (Patient / Personal Health Wallet) | Store signed VHL in Personal Health Wallet [ITI-YY3] Generate VHL | [ITI-YY3] Generate VHL response received by VHLHolder | . C. Present and Redeem Verifiable Health Link with PCF Consent Enforcement . | Process ID: PHW.C | BPMN Source: input/business-processes/PHW.C.bpmn | | Objective: Present a Verifiable Health Link ([ITI-YY4]), verify cryptographic signatures against a Trust Anchor’s trust list ([ITI-YY2]), request the health document manifest ([ITI-YY5]), query active PCF Consent ([ITI-108]), and enforce three-valued (permit | deny | unknown) ODRL consent evaluation with W3C PROV-O decision provenance. Trust-anchor neutral (WHO GDHCN is one possible Trust Anchor among others) and makes no IUA claim. | . | . | Activity ID | Lane / Actor | Task Name | IHE PCF / VHL Transaction & Conformance Profile | . | PHW.C.1 | VHL Holder (Patient / Personal Health Wallet) | Present VHL payload to Receiver [ITI-YY4] Provide VHL | [ITI-YY4] Provide VHL (https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/VHL/Requirements/UtilizeVHL) | . | PHW.C.2 | VHL Receiver (Verifier / Relying Party) | Request Trust Anchor key list [ITI-YY2] Retrieve Trust List with DID | [ITI-YY2] Retrieve Trust List with DID (https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/VHL/Requirements/RetrievePKIMaterial) | . | PHW.C.3 | Trust Anchor (e.g. GDHCN, national, or regional anchor) | Return signed trust list [ITI-YY2] (GDHCN or other Trust Anchor) | [ITI-YY2] Retrieve Trust List with DID (IHE.VHL.TrustAnchor) | . | PHW.C.4 | VHL Receiver (Verifier / Relying Party) | Verify VHL signature & request manifest [ITI-YY5] Retrieve Manifest | [ITI-YY5] Retrieve Manifest (https://profiles.ihe.net/ITI/VHL/Requirements/RequestVHLDocuments) | . | PHW.C.5 | VHL Sharer (grouped with PCF Consent Authorization Server) | Query active patient Consent [ITI-108] Access Consent: Search | [ITI-108] Access Consent: Search (GET [base]/Consent?patient=...&status=active) | . | PHW.C.6 | PCF Consent Registry | Return active PCF Consent Bundle [ITI-108] Access Consent | [ITI-108] Access Consent responder (IHE.PCF.consentRegistry), returning Consent.id and Consent.meta.versionId | . | PHW.C.7 | VHL Sharer (grouped with PCF Consent Authorization Server) | Evaluate PCF Consent (ODRL decide: permit / deny / unknown) & PROV-O log | consentToOdrl() + three-valued decide() (permit | deny | unknown) + W3C PROV-O prov:Activity citing Consent.id and Consent.meta.versionId | . | PHW.C.8 | VHL Sharer (grouped with PCF Consent Authorization Server) | Return authorized manifest & documents [ITI-YY5] Retrieve Manifest (permit) | [ITI-YY5] Retrieve Manifest (200 OK Bundle of DocumentReference / clinical resources when decision is permit) | . | PHW.C.9 | VHL Sharer (grouped with PCF Consent Authorization Server) | Refuse disclosure with OperationOutcome [ITI-YY5] (deny or unknown) | [ITI-YY5] Retrieve Manifest (403 Forbidden OperationOutcome when decision is deny or unknown) | . | PHW.C.10 | VHL Receiver (Verifier / Relying Party) | Process clinical documents or refusal notice [ITI-YY5] response | [ITI-YY5] Retrieve Manifest consumer (IHE.VHL.VHLReceiver) | . Data Sharing Agreement Processes (Server to Server) . Processes D to H implement a data sharing agreement (DSA) between a data provider and a data recipient. Each one is a technical process from the DSA process analysis for folio-assistant#2702 (P4, P5, P11, P12 and P13). The owner chose this IG as their home on 2026-10-30 (19:59Z). They apply to every agreement, whether it is computable (a W3C ODRL 2.2 Agreement derived from the legal text) or document-only (a signed PDF). The only difference is where the access rule comes from: the ODRL Agreement, or a configuration an administrator sets by hand from the PDF. What every process relies on: . | The agreement’s fixed-version URL. Each agreement version is published at an immutable URL, with its SHA-256, and catalogued as a DCAT 3 dcat:Distribution with spdx:checksum (DCAT 3 §6.8, §6.8.20). For a computable agreement this URL is also the ODRL uid. Tokens, grants, Consents and audit records cite this URL, never a “latest” URL. | Grants are W3C Verifiable Credentials 2.0. A grant cites the agreement through relatedResource (VC DM 2.0 §5.3), and its status is a W3C Bitstring Status List entry. litlfred/smart-trust-tools verifies it. | Pluggable trust anchors. WHO GDHCN is one option. The others are a national X.509 PKI, the party’s own did:web, or a local list. UDAP, as profiled by HL7 SSRAA, is approved (owner, 2026-10-30 20:28Z) for X.509 certificate-based registration and authentication, which fits a national X.509 PKI as the anchor. OpenID Federation is out of scope. | No invented fields. Where no standard has a slot, the text says so as a gap or open point. | . | # | Process Name | Process ID | DSA process | Objectives | . | D | Register a Server Client under a Data Sharing Agreement | PHW.D | P4 | Register the recipient’s server as an OAuth client (RFC 7591, UDAP via HL7 SSRAA, or by an administrator), authenticated by mTLS (RFC 8705) or a JWT assertion (RFC 7523; with UDAP, private_key_jwt with an x5c chain), and record which agreement versions it may act under. | . | E | Server-to-Server Access under a Data Sharing Agreement | PHW.E | P5 | Issue a short-lived, key-bound token (DPoP, RFC 9449) for an RFC 9396 authorization_details request whose identifier (§2.2) is the agreement’s fixed-version URL, after the access decision. | . | F | Access Decision under a Data Sharing Agreement | PHW.F | P11 | Run permits() on the verified grant and the agreement. A consent-based agreement also needs an active PCF Consent. The result is permit, deny or unknown, and unknown is never permit. | . | G | Audit, Provenance and Duty Checks under a Data Sharing Agreement | PHW.G | P12 | Record each decision as a W3C PROV-O record that cites the agreement, and as an IHE ATNA audit event ([ITI-20]). Record duty fulfilment and review it. | . | H | Revocation and Suspension under a Data Sharing Agreement | PHW.H | P13 | Stop grants (Bitstring Status List), tokens and clients (RFC 7009), and keys (trust list or CRL). | . The RFC 9396, RFC 9449, RFC 8693, W3C VC 2.0, W3C Bitstring Status List and DCAT 3 sections were checked against the published specifications on 2026-10-30. D. Register a Server Client under a Data Sharing Agreement . | Process ID: PHW.D | BPMN Source: input/business-processes/PHW.D.bpmn | Objective: Register the data recipient’s server as an OAuth client of the data provider’s authorization server. ATNA is reached in the same way the VHL profile reaches it. It expires (exp, claim key 4), and the VHL Sharer can stop serving the link. Verifiable Health Link Requests under an Existing Data Sharing Agreement . The VHL Sharer is the organisation or system that holds the documents. It may already have a data sharing agreement with the organisation or application that receives a VHL. It cites the agreement’s fixed-version URL, the receiver, the purpose of use, and the documents released (or the refusal). This follows the VHL profile’s own ATNA grouping: Vol 1 §1:XX.3 requires the VHL Sharer and the VHL Receiver to be grouped with an ATNA Secure Node or Secure Application for [ITI-YY5], and §1:XX.6.1 gives that grouping its audit logging. VHL itself says the Sharer SHOULD log access (ITI-YY5 §2:3.YY5.5.6) and MAY record the Audit Event – Accessed Health Data (ITI-YY5 §2:3.YY5.4.1.7). Under an agreement, the event is always recorded. IHE BALP needs owner approval (Trial Implementation). The PROV-O record of process G (PHW.G.1) cites the same agreement URL, so the ATNA log and the PROV log agree. Open points (owner): . | The lookup has no standard element. No existing VHL, OAuth or VC element maps a verified receiver to an agreement. The mapping is the Sharer’s own configuration, keyed by the agreement’s fixed-version URL, the same configuration as PHW.D.6. No field is invented. | Several agreements with one receiver. This is not decided. The Sharer may hold more than one agreement with the same receiver, and process I does not say which one applies, or whether all must permit. | Purpose of use in the audit event. With the SSRAA option, the purpose can come from the token request: purpose_of_use, a required array of codes in the hl7-b2b extension of the receiver’s JWT client assertion (SSRAA §5.2.1.1; HL7 v3 PurposeOfUse is encouraged, §5.2.1.2). SSRAA does not constrain the access token’s format (§5.2.3), so the Sharer has the purpose directly when its own authorization server issued the token; how a separate authorization server would pass it on is not specified. Without SSRAA, [ITI-YY5] carries no purpose, and it comes from the agreement or from the PCF Consent recorded at [ITI-YY3] (Consent.provision.purpose). Which source the event records, and which one wins when they differ, is open. | Possible ballot comments. The VHL Verifiable Credential Option example uses issuanceDate and expirationDate, which are VC 1.1 terms. VC 2.0 uses validFrom and validUntil. In the OAuth with SSRAA Option example (ITI-YY5 §2:3.YY5.4.1.4), the decoded client assertion gives purpose_of_use as a single string, where SSRAA §5.2.1.1 requires an array, and the token request omits the udap=1 parameter that SSRAA §5.2.2.2 requires. VHL says its workflow is informative and SSRAA takes precedence. | consent_policy in hl7-b2b. SSRAA §5.2.1.1 lets a client name policy URIs (consent_policy) and FHIR Consent URLs (consent_reference) in its token request. Whether a receiver may name the agreement’s fixed-version URL there, to choose among several agreements (point 2), is not decided; process I does not use it, and nothing is added. | . 1975.title: data-models-and-exchange
1975.content: . This section contains the data models and data exchange protocols with actors and transactions defined. It is part of the L3 machine-readable knowledge representation. The pages included in this section are described below. | Actors - A list and description of software or human entities that interact with the system, derived from business requirements defined in the L2. | Sequence Diagrams - Sequence diagrams depicting the interactions between system actors, in order, derived from business processes in the L2. | Transactions - A defined list of system transactions at an atomic level for each actor along with narrative, capability statements, structure definition, questionnaires, document bundles and composition. It may also refer to transactions in other implementation guides. | Logical Models - A StructureDefinition resource that describes data element definitions and their associated rules of usage, derived from the data dictionary in the L2. | Indicators and Measures - A thematic list of indicators defined in the implementation guide that link to L1 and L2 guidance documents. | . Design Documentation -DRAFT- . The documentation below details how to use this IG to execute the decision logic and the resources required to do so including PlanDefinitions, ActivityDefinitions, ValueSets, and Libraries. PlanDefinitions . insert content here has been represented as a FHIR PlanDefinition conformant to the FHIR Clinical Practice Guidelines Implementation guide CPG-ComputablePlanDefinition. For example, there is a PlanDefinition for Hepatitis A, Measles, etc. The intention behind this design is for each implementation to utilize only the antigens that are required for their national/local context, as many countries have national vaccine routines, which may leverage the WHO guidance. The aim of this content was to be adaptable for those contexts. These PlanDefinitions can be found in the Artifact Index . ActivityDefinitions . To represent the activities that need to be carried out, this implementation guide follows the workflow patterns established by the base FHIR specification. Each antigen represented as a PlanDefinition will be processed to produce ActivityDefnitions conform to the FHIR Clinical Practice Guidelines Implementation guide CPG-ActivityProfiles. FHIR Library . The FHIR Library contains a base64 encoded CQL library which represents the decision logic as a series of boolean clauses. Each PlanDefinition and Measure will reference a Library from which each decision point can be made and specify which expression from the CQL is used to trigger a decision in PlanDefinition or where to retrieve data to create the MeasureReport in the Measure, repsectively. ValueSets . Many of the ValueSets used in this IG are from CPG on FHIR and the IPS. There are a number of generated ValueSets based on the user scenarios detailed in this IG. There is one exception to that format which is the vaccine libraries, which map the codes between a variety of different systems including SNOMED GPS and WHO ATC in order to allow implementers to search for any vaccine which might be applicable to their user. 1998.title: Decision-support Logic
1998.content: . This page describes the decision support logic included in the WHO Digital Adaptation Kit (DAK) for [insert health domain here](link forthcoming). The decision-support logic component provides the decision logic and algorithms, as well as the scheduling of services, in accordance with WHO guidelines. The decision logic and algorithms in this implementation guide deconstruct the recommendations within the [insert health domain here] guidelines and guidance into a machine readable format that clearly labels the inputs and outputs that would be operationalized in a digital decision-support system. 9739.title: User Scenarios
9739.content: . Component 3 in the Digital Adaptation Kit (link forthcoming) includes user scenarios, which are narratives that describe how the different personas may interact with each other. The user scenarios are only illustrative and are intended to give an idea of a typical workflow. How to interpret user scenarios . User scenarios can be helpful tools not only to better understand the context in which a digital tool would operate, but also for some insights into what key data elements would need to be recorded and accounted for in the database. Additionally, the context in which the tool would operate, illuminated by the user scenarios, provides insight into some functional and non-functional requirements that the system would also need. As examples, the scenarios identify: key data elements that need to be recorded and/or calculated; decision-support logic that can be automated in the system; key functional and non-functional requirements that should be included in the system, and adolescent-specific considerations that should be accounted for. 10456.content: . Functional Requirements . Functional requirements describe the capabilities the system must have in order to meet the end-users’ needs and achieve tasks within the business process. These requirements are taken from Component 8 and Web Annex D of the WHO Digital Adaptation Kit for [insert health domain here] (link forthcoming). Please note that these are not exhaustive lists and should be modified according to context and user persona needs . Non-functional Requirements . Non-functional requirements provide the general attributes and features of the digital system to ensure usability and overcome technical and physical constraints. Examples of non-functional requirements include ability to work offline, multiple language settings and password protection.
